findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes
findings.body: The legacy write runs in a goroutine but uses a context derived from the request ctx (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Once the HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy Create (and the same pattern in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, lines 110, 135, 163) can fail spuriously with 'context canceled' before it completes. The legacy write is then silently dropped, which defeats the purpose of the 'safe measure' write. Detach from cancellation with context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout.

findings.title: Legacy Create receives the same obj that Storage.Create already mutated, concurrently
findings.body: `obj` is passed to `d.Storage.Create` synchronously and then to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine. Storage create implementations commonly mutate the object (name generation, resourceVersion, timestamps). The goroutine reads and possibly mutates the same object concurrently with any remaining work on the request path, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before the async legacy call.

findings.title: Legacy write failures in Create are only recorded as a metric, never logged
findings.body: In the Create goroutine the legacy error is passed to recordLegacyDuration but never logged. With writes now fire-and-forget, the metric is the only signal, and nothing identifies which object failed to reach legacy storage. Other methods also lack logging on the async path. Failures in the async safety writes should be logged with object identity.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the per-call logger
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` discards the `log` built just above with name/kind/method values. Downstream logs from the storage and legacy calls lose the request-specific fields that the other methods keep.

findings.title: Delete records the object name as the kind label on the storage duration metric
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` where the kind (`options.Kind`) is expected, as used on every other call. This corrupts the metric's label cardinality and makes per-kind dashboards wrong; each deleted object creates a new label value.

findings.title: Update records a Storage failure as a legacy duration metric
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`, not `recordStorageDuration`. Storage failures are counted against the legacy store, and the storage metric is never incremented for these failures, so both dashboards are wrong.

findings.title: Legacy Update reuses objInfo from the Storage update in a goroutine
findings.body: `objInfo` is consumed by `d.Storage.Update` synchronously and then passed to `d.Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations may be stateful or read the old object they were given. Calling UpdatedObject again concurrently and out of band with the request can race and can apply the change against the legacy store's old object, which may differ from unified storage. The previous implementation resolved the updated object once and passed it explicitly, and this change removes that.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy duration through the storage metric
findings.body: The async legacy path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. Legacy timings and failures are counted as storage. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`, as the other legacy goroutines do.

findings.title: Create error case sets up a legacy expectation but no storage expectation
findings.body: In the 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case, the mock expectation is attached to the legacy store (setupLegacyFn) and setupStorageFn is nil. Mode 3 calls Storage.Create first, so the storage mock has no expectation and the test fails for the wrong reason or panics. The expectation should be on storage. The test also never checks that the legacy write happens in the success case.

findings.title: Tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The mode 3 tests configure legacy mock expectations (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) but never assert they were called, and the legacy calls now run in goroutines that may not finish before the test returns. The tests therefore pass whether or not the legacy write happens, which is the core behaviour of this PR. Tests should wait for or synchronise with the goroutine and assert the legacy calls with AssertExpectations.

findings.title: Tests now share one global Prometheus registry
findings.body: The PR removes the per-test `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` in Mode1 Get and makes mode 3 tests use the package-level `p`. NewDualWriter registers metrics on the given registry, so every test now registers into the same registry. If the metrics are registered with MustRegister this will panic with AlreadyRegistered on the second test. Each test should use a fresh registry.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration runs assert immediately on legacy state that is written asynchronously
findings.body: In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a goroutine after the unified storage write returns. doPlaylistTests then checks the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint immediately after k8s creates or updates, for example listing legacy results after creating playlists. Those checks can run before the async legacy write lands, making the new mode 3 subtests flaky. The tests should poll or wait for the legacy side to converge in mode 3.

findings.title: Unrelated checksum entries added to go.work.sum
findings.body: The diff adds many go.sum lines for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, a prometheus-alertmanager fork, otel exporters and sdk v0.x, otlp proto, genproto rpc). These come from incidental dependency resolution, not from the mode 3 change. They should be dropped from this PR so the review and dependency surface stay focused.
